concept.name: Trading discipline
concept.definition: The consistent execution of a predefined trading process - entries, exits, sizing, and risk limits - regardless of emotional state or short-term outcomes. In the trading-psychology literature it is treated as a trainable skill of aligning behavior with plan, countering the documented biases that push traders off process.
concept.intuition: Discipline is doing the boring, correct thing - taking the stop, skipping the marginal setup - especially on the days you least want to.
concept.mechanics: Built through explicit written rules, checklists, pre-committed exits, position-sizing formulas, and review routines that convert intentions into habits; it is measured by rule-adherence rates rather than by P&L. Steenbarger frames discipline as self-coaching: structured practice, rehearsal, and feedback.
concept.failure_modes: Discipline cannot rescue a strategy without edge - flawless execution of a losing system produces consistent losses. It also degrades under fatigue, tilt, and oversized positions, because emotional arousal overwhelms willpower-based control.
concept.misconceptions: Discipline is not stubbornness: holding a loser past its invalidation is not conviction but indiscipline. Nor is it a fixed personality trait; it is largely a property of well-designed routines and constraints.
concept.example: A trader's stop is hit during a news spike; she exits per plan instead of widening it, and her month-end review shows 98% rule adherence even in a losing month.

citations.source: Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page
